extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers; readers and writers interested in Montaigne's reflections on reading, writing, family governance, wills, and military practice
extracted.subtask_short: essayist guidance on writing and reading
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative principles and practical norms from Montaigne's essays about how to read and write, how to judge books and authors, plus related advice on wills, family administration, and military preparedness. Emphasizes method, humility, natural style, and pragmatic custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess writing by method rather than matter
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let none lay stress upon the matter I write, but upon my method in writing it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne asks readers to judge his manner and method of writing (how he handles thoughts and arranges ideas) rather than treat his essays as authoritative statements of exhaustive knowledge. He frames his work as a personal method rather than a definitive body of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use borrowings sparingly and for invention (quality over quantity)
rubrics_metrics.description: “I do not number my borrowings, I weigh them; and had I designed to raise their value by number, I had made them twice as many.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations/borrowings should serve to raise or help the writer's invention; choose them for their aptness not to inflate apparent learning. Montaigne purposely selects a few famed authors rather than many minor references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote others to express what you cannot express yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: “I make others say for me, not before but after me, what, either for want of language or want of sense, I cannot myself so well express.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use other authors to articulate thoughts that are difficult to phrase; quotations can become part of the writer's voice. Montaigne also sometimes conceals authors to shield against censorious critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shelter weakness under reputable authorities when useful
rubrics_metrics.description: “I purposely conceal the author, to awe the temerity of those precipitate censors… I must shelter my own weakness under these great reputations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategically invoking or concealing authorities can be a rhetorical tactic to deflect unfair criticism or to strengthen arguments; Montaigne admits to doing this rather than feigning competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confess ignorance as a sign of sound judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: “The confession of ignorance is one of the finest and surest testimonies of judgment that I know.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honesty about limits of knowledge is presented as admirable and indicative of good judgment—better than pretending certainty on matters one does not master.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with a natural, personal pace and voice
rubrics_metrics.description: “I would that every one should see my natural and ordinary pace, irregular as it is; I suffer myself to jog on at my own rate.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne favors an unforced, personal, irregular tempo in writing—an authentic voice over an overworked or artificially polished style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overlabouring knowledge or style
rubrics_metrics.description: “My design is to pass over easily, and not laboriously, the remainder of my life; there is nothing that I will cudgel my brains about; no, not even knowledge, of what value soever.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not sacrifice ease and naturalness to excessive toil; excessive persistence can darken and tire judgment. Prefer lucidity and ease rather than forced erudition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read for honest diversion or for self-knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: “I seek, in the reading of books, only to please myself by an honest diversion; or, if I study, ‘tis for no other science than what treats of the knowledge of myself, and instructs me how to die and how to live well.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select reading according to personal pleasure or practical inward ends (self-knowledge, moral instruction) rather than purely to display erudition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not persist with unreadable or displeasing books
rubrics_metrics.description: “I do nothing without gaiety; continuation and a too obstinate endeavour, darkens, stupefies, and tires my judgment… If one book do not please me, I take another.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandon books that do not immediately engage; Montaigne values quick discernment and switching rather than stubbornly forcing comprehension through tedious books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer older, fuller works and sources you understand
rubrics_metrics.description: “I care not much for new ones, because the old seem fuller and stronger; neither do I converse much with Greek authors, because my judgment cannot do its work with imperfect intelligence of the material.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor time-tested classics over novelty; read in languages you can properly comprehend so your judgment can operate effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be modest in criticism and aware of your limits
rubrics_metrics.description: When Montaigne is disgusted with a work he admits: “my judgment does not believe itself… It is content with only securing itself from trouble and disorder; as to its own weakness, it frankly acknowledges and confesses it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should be humble—recognize when your understanding is superficial and avoid overconfident condemnation of great authors; accept mentorship from established judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let laws/custom govern succession unless manifest cause exists
rubrics_metrics.description: “The most judicious distribution of our goods, when we come to die, is, in my opinion, to let them be distributed according to the custom of the country; the laws have considered the matter better than we know how to do… it is against reason to abuse this liberty, in making it serve our own frivolous and private fancies.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estate distribution should generally follow customary legal rules rather than capricious personal adjustments; only substantial and manifest reasons (e.g., permanent deformity) justify violating ordinary descent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give weight to recent actions when making wills
rubrics_metrics.description: “The last action carries it, not the best and most frequent offices, but the most recent and present do the work.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that testators often reward or punish by immediate impressions—recent behavior tends to weigh heavily in last dispositions; hence wise planning should guard against impulsive changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide for mothers and allow maternal administration until children mature
rubrics_metrics.description: “‘Tis reasonable to leave the administration of affairs to the mothers, till the children are old enough, according to law… they ought to be plentifully provided for, to maintain themselves according to their quality and age.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues mothers should be allowed to manage affairs temporarily and should be suitably provided for, as indigence is especially unbecoming for them; family arrangements should consider maternal welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer habit and training with arms over sporadic use
rubrics_metrics.description: “‘Tis an ill custom… not to put on arms but just upon the point of the most extreme necessity… Our ancestors… never put off the other pieces so long as there was any work to be done.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soldiers and gentlemen should be accustomed to bearing arms continuously when duty requires it; habituation reduces burden and increases efficiency—sporadic arming leads to disorder and slower response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance armour protection with mobility; avoid overburdening equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne notes heavy armour can ‘load rather than secure’ and praises armours ‘so woven as to have all the scales fall over one another… did nothing hinder the motion of the body, and yet were of such resistance.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and select defensive equipment that preserves freedom of motion; excessively heavy or cumbersome armour can hinder movement and make the wearer more vulnerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military discipline and austerity produce stronger troops
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: the younger Scipio ordered soldiers to eat standing and unprepared food; Roman infantry carried provisions and incurred heavy burdens but marched long distances in formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardship, simple habits, and strict discipline (training to bear weight, endure weather, and live simply) produce more effective soldiers than comfort and indulgence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate personal skill and confidence over over-reliance on defensive devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Scipio’s admonition: ‘a Roman soldier ought to repose greater confidence in his right hand than in his left’ (i.e., skill over shield/armour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactical emphasis should be on ability and initiative rather than mere dependence on armour or defensive contrivances; training the individual is crucial.
